{"id": "3bbbe024-39e9-47ec-8f58-2e503f12acb1", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_Ng3kVfPVlH0yPzd90W1rQN", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"status\":\"SUCCESS\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/direct-connect-asymmetric-routing\",\"content\":\"# How can I resolve asymmetric routing issues when I create a VPN as a backup to a Direct Connect connection in a transit gateway?\\n\\nI have an AWS Direct Connect connection. The Direct Connect gateway is associated with an AWS Transit Gateway. I created a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup to the Direct Connect connection, but I have asymmetric routing issues. \\n\\n---\\n\\nShort description\\n-----------------\\n\\nWhen you use a virtual private network (VPN) connection as a backup to Direct Connect, asymmetric routing issues can occur. Asymmetric routing occurs when network traffic enters through one connection and exits through another connection. If the traffic that's received isn't logged in your stateful table, then network devices, such as firewalls, can drop packets.\\n\\nResolution\\n----------\\n\\n### Outbound traffic from AWS to your network\\n\\nUse the following best practices for outbound traffic from AWS to your network:\\n\\n*   Use [Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpn/latest/s2svpn/VPNRoutingTypes.html#vpn-static-dynamic) to configure the VPN with dynamic routing.\\n*   Make sure that your devices advertise the same or less specific prefixes from on-premises to AWS with the VPN and Direct Connect. For example, 10.0.0.0/16 is less specific than 10.0.0.0/24.\\n*   For a prefix length that's the same value, AWS sends on-premises traffic to your network with a higher preference value for Direct Connect over VPN connections. For the AWS Transit Gateway, use a static route that points to a VPN attachment rather than a dynamically propagated Direct Connect gateway route.\\n*   For Direct Connect that you deploy with dynamic VPN as backup, it's not a best practice to use AS PATH prepending. If the prefixes are the same, then use Direct Connect routes regardless of the AS PATH prepend length.\\n\\nFor more information, see [Routing](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work.html#tgw-routing-overview).\\n\\n### Inbound traffic from your network to AWS\\n\\nUse the following best practices for inbound traffic from your network to AWS:\\n\\n*   Configure your network device preference to send return traffic through the Direct Connect connection.\\n*   If the prefixes that are advertised from AWS to your network device are the same for Direct Connect and VPN, then use the BGP local preference attribute. The BGP local preference attribute forces your device to send outbound traffic through the Direct Connect connection toward AWS. Set the Direct Connect path with a higher local preference value, and set a lower preference for VPN. For example, set local preference to 200 for Direct Connect and 100 for VPN.\\n\\n**Important:** For Direct Connect allowed prefixes that are summarized and less specific than the routes advertised through VPN, network devices prefer the routes received through VPN.\\n\\nSee the following example scenario:\\n\\n*   The transit gateway propagated routes are VPC-A CIDR 10.0.0.0/16, VPC-B CIDR 10.1.0.0/16, and VPC-C 10.2.0.0/16.\\n*   To accommodate the [20-prefix quota](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/limits.html), the summarized prefix on the Direct Connect gateway [allowed prefixes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/directconnect/latest/UserGuide/allowed-to-prefixes.html) is 10.0.0.0/14.\\n\\nFor each virtual private cloud (VPC) over VPN, Direct Connect advertises the Direct Connect gateway prefix 10.0.0.0/14 and the VPN transit gateway advertises the /16 CIDRs.\\n\\nTo resolve this issue, insert the summarized Direct Connect gateway route into the transit gateway route table. For example, add a static route 10.0.0.0/14 that points to a VPC attachment so that the transit gateway advertises the summarized network over VPN. Your network devices receive the same prefix from Direct Connect and VPN. Then, configure your gateway to filter out the specific prefixes that are received. Make sure that only the summarized prefix is installed in the routing table from the VPN peer. Depending on vender specifications, there are different options to filter out routes, such as route-maps, prefix-lists, and router-filter-lists.\\n\\nTraffic from your network to AWS reaches the transit gateway route table. The gateway does a lookup to select the most specific routes from each VPC attachment.\\n\\nSee the following example:\\n\\n*   Attachment A that points to VPC-A CIDR is 10.0.0.0/16.\\n*   Attachment B that points to VPC-B CIDR is 10.1.0.0/16.\\n*   Attachment C that points to VPC-C CIDR is 10.2.0.0/16.\\n\\nRelated information\\n-------------------\\n\\n[Route priority](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Route_Tables.html#route-tables-priority)\\n\\n[How do I configure Direct Connect and VPN failover with Transit Gateway?](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/dx-configure-dx-and-vpn-failover-tgw)\",\"total_length\":4780,\"start_index\":0,\"end_index\":4780,\"truncated\":false,\"redirected_url\":null,\"error_code\":null}]}}"}]}], "label": "Read AWS knowledge center article on resolving asymmetric routing with VPN backup to Direct Connect."}

{"id": "7b4cfba0-938a-4ddb-9838-9783af148401", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's how AWS decides and how to keep routing symmetric.

**Which path wins**

For a VGW receiving routes over both a Direct Connect private VIF and a Site-to-Site VPN:

1. **Longest prefix match always wins first**, regardless of which path it came in on. If your VPN happens to advertise a more specific prefix than Direct Connect (common if DX is summarized to fit the 20-prefix allowed-prefix quota), traffic will route over the "backup" VPN even while DX is healthy.
2. **If prefix lengths are equal, AWS prefers the Direct Connect-learned route over the VPN-learned route.** This holds true for both directions AWS controls internally — it's the same precedence Transit Gateway and VGW apply.

So in a healthy, correctly-configured setup with matching prefix lengths, DX is preferred automatically, and VPN only takes over once DX actually goes down (BGP session drops or prefixes withdrawn).

**Avoiding asymmetric routing**

The risk is each direction being controlled by a different party, so they can disagree:

- **Outbound (AWS → on-prem), controlled by AWS:**
  - Make sure your on-prem router advertises the **same or less-specific prefixes** over both DX and VPN — if VPN advertises a more specific route than the DX allowed-prefix summary, AWS will send return traffic over VPN regardless of DX being up.
  - Don't use AS_PATH prepending on the DX advertisement as a "make VPN look better" trick — if prefix lengths match, AWS uses DX regardless of AS_PATH length, so prepending only causes confusion without changing AWS's preference.

- **Inbound (on-prem → AWS), controlled by your router:**
  - AWS advertises the **same prefixes** from the VGW over both DX and VPN, so by default your router has no strong signal unless you configure one.
  - Set **BGP local preference** on your CPE: higher for the DX-learned routes (e.g., 200), lower for VPN-learned routes (e.g., 100). This forces your side to prefer sending to AWS over DX, matching AWS's own preference.

- **Watch for prefix-length mismatches** specifically — this is the most common real-world cause of asymmetric routing in this setup, more so than BGP attribute misconfiguration. If DX has to summarize due to the prefix-count limit, insert a matching summarized static route into your VPN advertisement (and filter out the more specific ones) so both paths present identical prefix lengths to AWS.

Want me to pull up the actual BGP attributes currently being advertised on your VIF and VPN to check whether you have a prefix-length or local-preference mismatch right now?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
